title: "DropMyRights"
subtitle: A tiny Microsoft tool runs risky programs with reduced privileges
description: A Christmas Day episode on DropMyRights, a small free utility by Microsoft's Michael Howard that runs chosen Internet-facing programs, like your browser and email, as a non-admin even while you stay admin. Steve explains Windows' access-token security model, software restriction policies, and how this compares to UNIX's "log in limited, escalate when needed." Plus a DNSChanger trojan that spoofs DHCP, Firefox 2's last version losing anti-phishing, and the YubiKey as a 32-character static password.

beats.t: Today we cover DropMyRights, a poor man's Sandboxie that runs chosen applications without admin rights even while you're admin.

In the news, the DNSChanger trojan has a fascinating new version. It installs a valid NDIS network driver that gives it raw sockets, then pretends to be a DHCP server. One infected machine on a LAN races the real DHCP server to answer a booting machine's request, and if it wins, it reconfigures that machine's DNS to a malicious server.
So on any LAN, even WiFi at Starbucks, one infected laptop can redirect everyone else's DNS. A malicious DNS can serve correct answers for most sites but send BankofAmerica.com to a clone.
It's not automatic just from being on a Starbucks network.
No, nothing against Starbucks. It's if the trojan is on a machine there. Default Windows uses DHCP, so a rogue DHCP server anywhere on the LAN can answer.
Does a static IP avoid this?
Yes, since you're not using DHCP at all, nothing sets your DNS. You can also map a MAC address to a fixed IP in the router to get static assignment through DHCP, which is handy for port forwarding.

beats.title: Rogue DHCP
beats.t: A rogue DHCP server handing out malicious DNS is a real attack. Modern switches offer "DHCP snooping" to block unauthorized DHCP replies, and HTTPS certificate checks limit the damage of a spoofed DNS answer.
Firefox 2's final version ships December 16 and loses its anti-phishing feature, because it used the first anti-phishing API that Google will no longer support.
You shouldn't be using 2 anyway.

Version 3 has been out since June. If you depend on anti-phishing, you might stay on the supported 2 before this last one, but you'll be on an unsupported browser with no security updates. Better to move to 3.

chapters.title: The YubiKey as a Static Password

beats.t: YubiKey news. Yubico's new personalization tool lets you take over your key with your own AES secret, or set it to emit a fixed 32-character random password instead of a one-time code.

That's useful for offline authentication, like TrueCrypt whole-drive encryption at pre-boot, where there's no Internet for the normal one-time mode. Thirty-two random ASCII characters is about 192 bits, seriously strong, and since passwords are entered blanked, nobody sees it.
You could use it for your WPA key.

Exactly. Put the cursor in a guest's password field, touch the button, confirm, and they're on your network without ever learning the key. Keystroke loggers are the only caveat, and they're not an issue at pre-boot.
And Password Safe now supports the YubiKey in full one-time-password mode too.
They're going to sell a lot of YubiKeys.

Earl Pearce bought SpinRite in 2006, saw no miracles, then hit an unmountable-boot-volume blue screen so brief he had to video the screen and single-step it to read it. After a couple of drive-heat warnings, SpinRite fixed it and the system worked great. He called me Gandalf reborn.
I didn't realize DropMyRights was a side project by a Microsoft employee.

It's a tiny utility leveraging technology built into Windows since XP. The security model has two kinds of objects: an access token, a collection of rights you get when you log in, and security descriptors, the requirements attached to files, directories, processes, threads, registry keys, services, printers, shares and more.

Any process you run inherits your rights, and nearly everything it does is checked against each object's descriptor. There are many privileges: restore, backup, load driver, shutdown, debug, even change the system time. Debug is powerful, letting a process read another's memory. Backup and restore bypass other access restrictions, since a backup must read everything.
The granddaddy is admin. Malware wants admin rights to write to system32, terminate processes, disable the Windows firewall, or delete keys under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE.
XP added Software Restriction Policies, letting policies apply by an executable's hash, name or location, which corporate IT uses to lock systems down.

Michael Howard, a security-minded Microsoft engineer, blogged four years ago that he runs as admin but realized some programs, like IE, are too dangerous to have full admin rights. So he wrote DropMyRights.

You prefix a shortcut's command with dropmyrights.exe, passing the real program as its argument. It creates a process token with non-admin rights and runs the program under them. So Firefox and Eudora run as non-admin while the rest of your session stays admin.
It's like Run As in reverse.
Exactly. Instead of a limited user escalating, you're an admin de-escalating specific apps.
On UNIX and Linux you always log in as a normal user and escalate with sudo when needed. Wouldn't that be better on Windows?

Absolutely, but the two systems came from different directions. UNIX had a superuser and normal users from day one, so applications assume they're not root. Windows grew from DOS and Windows 95, where there was one all-powerful user, so developers running as admin never tested as non-admin, and their software broke for limited users.
It really goes back to DOS: one user, one process.
Software restriction policy defines five levels: trusted (essentially admin), normal (non-admin), constrained, untrusted, and disallowed. DropMyRights offers normal, constrained, or untrusted.

Untrusted is so restricted that not even Notepad runs. Constrained is sketchy too: HKEY_CURRENT_USER is read-only, the user profile directory is inaccessible, and even SSL negotiation fails, so you can't run a browser. Just dropping to normal removes admin privileges, which is what you want, and Firefox and Eudora run fine.

I asked Ronen why Sandboxie doesn't do this. He said it already strips many privileges from sandboxed programs: restore, backup, load driver, debug, and system time. He didn't want to duplicate another tool, but he's adding the full DropMyRights capability in the next Sandboxie beta, so you can optionally run a sandbox as non-admin.
DropMyRights still matters for 64-bit users who can't run Sandboxie, or anyone not using it. If you run as admin, use it on your Internet-facing programs.
Run As is too inconvenient for people to run as limited users, though Vista makes it easier.

Vista's User Account Control is the evolution of this: you log in limited and briefly elevate. For those of us not on Vista, DropMyRights is a clean, weightless way to run risky apps with reduced rights.
I suspect you could even do this with policies alone, no DropMyRights.exe, by creating extra categories beyond trusted and disallowed. I want to poke at that.

beats.title: Where this led
beats.t: Internet Explorer later gained "Protected Mode," which ran the browser with low integrity rights automatically, and UAC made elevate-when-needed the norm. Running everyday programs with least privilege remains a core security practice.

quiz.q: Why do many Windows programs break when run as a non-admin?
options: Developers ran as admin and never tested with limited rights
quiz.explain: UNIX apps assume they're not root from the start.

quiz.q: Why is the "untrusted" restriction level nearly useless?
options: It's so restricted that not even Notepad will run
quiz.explain: Dropping to "normal" is enough to remove admin rights.

quiz.q: What can a YubiKey set to a 32-character static password be used for?
options: Offline authentication like a TrueCrypt pre-boot password or a WPA key
quiz.explain: It's about 192 random bits and entered blanked.

quiz.q: Why does admin privilege matter so much to malware?
options: It can write to system32, kill processes, disable the firewall and edit HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
quiz.explain: Running risky apps as non-admin limits the damage.
